rv.q: The Mirror and the Light dramatises – supremely well – the concluding volume in Hilary Mantel’s award-winning trilogy about Thomas Cromwell, the son of a Putney blacksmith who rose to be the fixer-in-chief at the court of King Henry VIII.
This is an urgent, propulsive journey through the dense thickets of Tudor court politics, and a wider rumination on what happens when indispensability becomes a liability rather than an asset.

This is absolutely not a weepie tragedy, but a fast, often very funny political thriller...But although Herrin’s production zips through all this in a relatively short space of time, it never feels perfunctory.
It is an accomplished translation from page to stage, exemplary in its bold decision to lose some memorable passages to drive forward the action.
Miles remains superb – urbane, resourceful and stoical. He has huge gravitas and steely charisma too.
At its best, Jeremy Herrin’s deft production embraces this to advantage: the sorrow around Jane’s death is beautifully, wordlessly evoked through a forest of candles.
The new stage incarnation reactivates some of that excitement.

Unmoored from its previous parts, The Mirror And The Light is perhaps inevitably bogged down by heavy exposition. But once the plot gets going – charting the rise and fall of Thomas Cromwell – it proves a solidly absorbing tale. Ben Miles returns as the ambitious Cromwell, suave, smooth, and with impeccable timing for a tart retort.
Instead, this is a brisk, colourful cavalcade: short on nuance, yet undeniably entertaining.

This is an accomplished production in many ways, but, almost too focused on the task at hand, it lacks emotional heft, skips too quickly over key scenes and can’t ever fully escape the shadow of the axe.
This is all very fine, but there’s no grief, no great release at the end, just a dull sense of a historical juggernaut juddering to a halt.
It’s good enough, but it could have been so much more.
Herrin’s ideally marshaled stage productions of Mantel’s re-invention of Cromwell have helped create a complete dramatic — in every sense — reappraisal of history.
His charisma and subtlety give the play its range; he is the main reason for catching this production, as alive to the richness of Cromwell's character as Mantel is in her books.

Aurora Dawson Hunte as Elizabeth Seymour and the company of The Mirror and the Light. Oram's set design is a masterstroke, too, but he erodes its effect by togging up the actors in pretty English Heritage-style period costume, hopelessly at odds with his brilliant contemporary staging (and one cannot help but wonder, ultimately, whose decision...
The general effect is impressive, but with so much promise unfulfilled in the other characters it prompts a searching question of what might have been.
Ultimately, Mantel's powerful prose is not quite realised in this entertaining, but rather safe adaptation.
The problem is a narrative compression so extreme that the story barely has time to breathe, paired with an ensemble overly prone to shouting.
Still it all just amounts to a rather flat narrative pageant, not the anticipated engagement with human darkness, gory humour, mirrors and light on souls.
This adaptation delivers as it should and completes a masterly transfer from one medium to another, with the televisual finale still to come to complete the set.
If this is a lightweight rendering of a heavyweight novel, it simply proves that a labour of love is not necessarily a good night out.

cn.t: Critics find this conclusion to Mantel's Cromwell trilogy a solid but lesser achievement than its predecessors, weighed down by exposition yet propelled by Ben Miles' commanding performance and Jeremy Herrin's clear direction.

vr.q: Ben Miles performance as this complex man... is a tour de force
